newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Labour party now favours wealth.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Labour party now favours wealth.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour party, which once promised to "squeeze the rich until the pips squeak," will look after millionaires if it wins power at the election.

After 18 bitter years of opposition, Labour has distanced itself so much from its socialist past that its economic policies are virtually indistinguishable from those of Prime Minister John Major's Conservatives.

The transformation reached a climax in January when the party promised that there would be no increase in income tax rates and said it would live within the tight public spending constraints imposed by the Conservative government.

"You would need to go back to the 1950s to find such uniform agreement across the two major political parties on the conduct of economic policy," says David Walton, senior economist at Goldman Sachs in London.

Michael Saunders, an economist at Salomon Brothers, says the two parties are offering almost identical policies -- "The same spending plans, ambitions (but no commitments) for lower taxes and probably the same inflation target."
Labour's policies have changed beyond recognition since its last prime minister, James Callaghan, was ousted from Number 10, Downing Street by Margaret Thatcher in 1979.

Whereas Labour finance minister Dennis Healey famously pledged in 1974 to squeeze the rich and raised the top rate of income tax to 83 percent, present-day "New Labour" is anxious to reassure the wealthy that they have nothing to fear.
"I want to see us create more millionaires than Mrs Thatcher, provided they pay fair taxes," said Mike O'Brien, Labour's shadow economic secretary, in a recent interview.

Finance spokesman Gordon Brown has since promised to leave untouched the income tax rates he would inherit from the Conservatives -- a standard rate of 23 percent and top rate of 40 percent, both low by international standards.

Labour does not plan to renationalise key industries such as telecommunications, which were privatised by the Conservatives, and will not repeal stiff curbs on the power of trade unions, whose influence on Labour policy has been diminished.

Labour leader Tony Blair has assiduously courted business leaders, offering them a "new deal" under which Labour would leave intact the Conservative government's reforms in industrial relations and its measures to liberalise the economy.
In return, he asked business to cooperate with a Labour government on a new agenda for the 21st century, working on education, welfare reform and the country's infrastructure.
Blair and Brown pledge "iron discipline" in public spending and have indicated they will adopt an inflation target broadly similar to the 2.5 percent goal set by the Conservatives.

"Labour will be the party of sound finance, providing a stable platform for business investment and protecting families from high inflation and mortgage rates," the party said in a recent policy document.

The main remaining differences between the two main parties over economic policy are Labour's plans to introduce a national minimum wage, to sign up to the European Union's Social Chapter on workers' rights and to impose a windfall tax on the profits of privatised utility companies.
The one-off windfall tax would be used to finance a programme to reduce youth unemployment by 250,000.

Business leaders fear a minimum wage and membership of the Social Chapter would increase business costs and lead to higher unemployment. "We think they are wrong on those two issues and we will go on telling them," said Ruth Lea, head of policy at the Institute of Directors.
Labour appears to be slightly more sympathetic to the idea of a single European currency than the Conservatives, but it has avoided making specific commitments.

Like Major, Blair has promised a referendum if the government decided that joining a single currency would be in Britain's interest. Foreign affairs spokesman Robin Cook said at the weekend it would be hard for Britain to stay out of the single currency if it proved a success. Economists say the acid test in the first two years of a Labour administration will be whether or not it can maintain control of public spending.
It will face enormous pressure from public sector workers, whose pay has been virtually frozen in recent years, to boost their incomes.
Labour will have difficulty in reconciling its pledges to improve education and health care and reform the welfare state with its commitment to curbing public expenditure.
The party argues that much can be done by using existing resources more effectively, such as by spending more on nurses and doctors and less on health service administrators.

"We must release resources from that part of the budget which is being spent on the consequences of economic failure -- an unreformed welfare state which traps whole families out of work, persistent long-term and youth unemployment and low wages caused by low skills," Brown said recently.
But Paul Johnson of the Institute for Fiscal Studies says the public spending commitments Labour has pledged to abide by are "almost inconceivably tight."

"If either party does keep to them, then it's going to mean a real squeeze in services like health and education," he said. "If that doesn't happen, taxes are likely to have to be higher than either is admitting."

Gavyn Davies, chief economist at Goldman Sachs and a member of the Treasury's panel of independent economic advisers, said in a recent newspaper article that Blair and Brown were anxious to avoid a rise in the tax burden.
"They recalled that the 1974-79 Labour government never recovered from losing control of the purse strings in its first six months and resolved that this was not going to happen to them."
